questions.question: What are truthy and falsy values in Python, and when should a comparison be explicit?
questions.title: Truthy, Falsy, and Explicit Checks
questions.direct_answer: Python treats `False`, `None`, numeric zero, and empty containers as falsy; most other values are truthy. Use a direct truth test for presence, but compare explicitly when zero, empty, and missing have different meanings.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Falsy built-ins include `False`, `None`, zero, and empty strings or containers.
Most non-empty and non-zero values are truthy.
Use `if items:` when empty and absent should follow the same path.
Use `is None` when missing is different from a valid empty or zero value.
Custom classes can define truth through `__bool__` or `__len__`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Truthiness is how Python turns an object into a Boolean result when it appears in `if`, `while`, `and`, `or`, or `not`. Calling `bool(value)` shows the same result directly. Truthiness does not change the original value; it only decides which branch a Boolean context takes.

The common falsy values are `False`, `None`, numeric zero, and empty values such as `''`, `[]`, `{}`, `set()`, and `()`. Most other objects are truthy, including non-zero numbers and non-empty containers. This lets `if items:` express the simple question, “does this collection contain anything?”

A truth test deliberately groups all falsy states. That is useful for `if not errors:` when an empty error collection is the only state that matters. It is wrong when the states have different meanings. For a timeout, `None` may mean “use the default” while `0` means “return immediately”; `if not timeout:` would incorrectly treat both alike.

Use `value is None` for the `None` singleton, `count == 0` for an exact numeric check, and `left == right` for value equality. Identity asks whether two references point to the same object, so ordinary values should not be compared with `is`. The condition should name the distinction the program needs to preserve.

A class can define `__bool__`; otherwise Python may use whether `__len__` returns zero. An object with neither behavior is truthy by default. Custom truth rules should stay unsurprising, because hiding several important states behind one Boolean result makes conditions difficult to read and easy to misuse.

beats.spokenText: The common falsy values are `False`, `None`, numeric zero, and empty values such as `''`, `[]`, `{}`, `set()`, and `()`. Most other objects are truthy, including non-zero numbers and non-empty containers. This lets `if items:` express the simple question, “does this collection contain anything?”

beats.recallRule: Use a truth test only when every falsy value is meant to follow the same path; otherwise test the exact state explicitly.

sections.title: One Boolean result can hide several data states
sections.content:
Truth testing is a protocol, not a list of hard-coded syntax exceptions. Python first asks an object for `__bool__`; if that method is unavailable, it may use whether `__len__` returns zero. Objects with neither behavior are true by default.

This flexibility makes conditions concise, but a condition should not erase information needed by the next step. API payloads frequently distinguish an omitted field (`None` or a missing key), an explicitly empty value, and a numeric zero. Those cases need explicit tests.

A condition is correct when its Boolean grouping matches the domain grouping, not merely when it passes a few common inputs.

sections.title: Ask the exact data question
sections.content:
| Intended question | Clear check | Distinction preserved |
|---|---|---|
| Does the collection contain items? | `if items:` | No: absent and empty may combine |
| Was no optional value supplied? | `if value is None:` | Yes: keeps `0`, `False`, and `''` |
| Is the count exactly zero? | `if count == 0:` | Yes: names the numeric case |
| Do two values compare equal? | `if left == right:` | Uses value equality |

sections.title: Preserve zero as a real timeout
List the falsy cases before shortening a condition
sections.content: Before changing `if result is None` to `if not result`, test `0`, `False`, `''`, `[]`, and `{}`. Use the shorter form only if every one of those values truly means the same thing.

questions.question: How do in and not in work with Python strings, collections, and dictionaries?
questions.title: Membership Tests with In and Not In
questions.direct_answer: `in` asks whether a container contains a value; `not in` negates that result. Dictionaries test keys, strings test substrings, and sets provide the clearest fast average membership lookup for hashable values.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: For lists and tuples, membership compares each element until one is equal.
For strings, membership checks for a substring, not only one character.
For dictionaries, membership checks keys unless `.values()` or `.items()` is used.
Sets and dictionaries usually provide average constant-time membership for hashable keys.
`not in` is the readable negation of the same membership test.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The expression `needle in container` asks the right-hand object whether it contains the value, and `needle not in container` negates that same result. The operator is shared syntax, but containment means something different for a sequence, string, mapping, or set.

For a list or tuple, membership compares elements from left to right until one is equal to the needle or the sequence ends. A successful search can stop early, but the general cost grows with the number of elements. This is the right model when order or duplicate elements are still meaningful data.

For strings, membership checks a contiguous substring rather than a whole word. Therefore `'read' in 'reader'` is true, while case differences still matter. If the requirement is case-insensitive text, normalized Unicode, or whole-word matching, prepare or parse the text first instead of expecting `in` to understand that linguistic rule.

For a dictionary, `'A17' in users` checks whether `'A17'` is a key; writing `.keys()` is unnecessary. Searching `users.values()` is an explicit value scan, while `('A17', 'Ada') in users.items()` asks whether that key-value pair exists. The chosen view should match the unit being searched.

Sets and dictionary keys normally use hashing for average `O(1)` membership, so they are useful for many repeated lookups. Their searched values must be hashable, and collision behavior means constant time is an average rather than an absolute guarantee. Converting a list to a set costs work and removes duplicates, so it is worthwhile only when those semantics and future lookups justify the conversion.

support.title: Search the intended dictionary surface
support.code:
users = {"A17": "Ada", "B04": "Bo"}

print("A17" in users)
print("Ada" in users)
print("Ada" in users.values())
print(("A17", "Ada") in users.items())

print("read" in "reader")

beats.spokenText: Sets and dictionary keys normally use hashing for average `O(1)` membership, so they are useful for many repeated lookups. beats.recallRule: Read `in` as containment defined by the right-hand object: elements for sequences and sets, substrings for strings, and keys for dictionaries.

sections.title: The right-hand object defines containment
sections.content:
The expression `needle in container` delegates containment behavior to the right-hand object. Built-in sequences compare candidates until a match is found. A dictionary exposes its keys as its normal iteration and membership surface, which is why key checks need no `.keys()` call.

Hash-based containers require hashable search keys. A set is useful when uniqueness is part of the model and membership is frequent; building a new set for one tiny lookup can cost more work than the original list scan.

String containment works on contiguous substrings. It is case-sensitive and does not split text into words, so domain-specific text matching may need normalization or a parser.

sections.title: What does membership inspect?
sections.content:
| Right-hand value | `needle in value` checks | Typical cost |
|---|---|---|
| `list` / `tuple` | Equal elements | Linear scan |
| `str` | Contiguous substring | Search depends on text and pattern |
| `set` | Hashable elements | Average constant time |
| `dict` | Keys | Average constant time |
| `dict.values()` | Equal values | Linear scan |
| `dict.items()` | `(key, value)` pairs | View membership rules |

sections.title: Check the intended dictionary surface
sections.content:
```python
users = {"A17": "Ada", "B04": "Bo"}

print("A17" in users)                 # True: key
print("Ada" in users)                 # False: not a key
print("Ada" in users.values())        # True: value
print(("A17", "Ada") in users.items()) # True: pair

roles = {"reader", "editor"}
print("editor" in roles)              # True
print("read" in "reader")            # True: substring
```

sections.title: Match the unit to the question
sections.content: `'he' in 'the report'` is true even though `he` is not a word there. If whole words matter, tokenize according to the text rules before testing membership.

questions.question: How does Python compare strings, lists, and tuples in order?
questions.title: Lexicographic Sequence Comparison in Python
questions.direct_answer: Python compares same-kind sequences lexicographically: it examines corresponding elements from left to right, stops at the first difference, and uses length only when the shared prefix is equal.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Sequence ordering compares corresponding elements from left to right.
The first unequal pair decides the result.
If one sequence is an exact prefix, the shorter sequence sorts first.
String ordering uses Unicode code points and is case-sensitive, not dictionary order.
Ordering unrelated types such as an integer and string raises `TypeError` in Python 3.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Python orders comparable strings, lists, and tuples lexicographically: it compares corresponding elements from left to right. This is a sequence rule rather than a total ordering over every Python object, so the element pair Python reaches must support the requested comparison.

For `(2026, 8, 31) < (2026, 9, 1)`, the equal years lead to `8 < 9`, which makes the expression true; the day values are never inspected. The same early decision means `[1, 'x'] < [2, object()]` succeeds through `1 < 2` without touching the incompatible later values.

When every compared element is equal and one sequence ends, the shorter sequence sorts first. That is why `[1, 2] < [1, 2, 0]` is true. If both sequences end together after equal elements, they compare equal rather than one being smaller.

Strings compare their characters using Unicode code-point order. It is deterministic and case-sensitive, but it is not automatically dictionary order for a language or locale. Python 3 also refuses arbitrary ordering such as `3 < '4'`; a list or tuple comparison raises `TypeError` if it reaches an element pair that cannot be ordered.

A tuple key turns lexicographic behavior into an explicit priority list. With `key=lambda user: (user['name'].casefold(), user['id'])`, the normalized name is primary and the ID breaks ties. `casefold()` helps with case-insensitive matching, while proper human-language collation may still require locale-aware tooling.

beats.cue: Define lexicographic comparison as a left-to-right process
beats.spokenText: Python orders comparable strings, lists, and tuples lexicographically: it compares corresponding elements from left to right. This is a sequence rule rather than a total ordering over every Python object, so the element pair Python reaches must support the requested comparison.

When every compared element is equal and one sequence ends, the shorter sequence sorts first. That is why `[1, 2] < [1, 2, 0]` is true. If both sequences end together after equal elements, they compare equal rather than one being smaller.

Python 3 also refuses arbitrary ordering such as `3 < '4'`; a list or tuple comparison raises `TypeError` if it reaches an element pair that cannot be ordered.

With `key=lambda user: (user['name'].casefold(), user['id'])`, the normalized name is primary and the ID breaks ties. `casefold()` helps with case-insensitive matching, while proper human-language collation may still require locale-aware tooling.

support.title: Order records by name and then ID
support.code:
users = [
    {"id": 3, "name": "Singh"},
    {"id": 2, "name": "ada"},
    {"id": 1, "name": "Ada"},
]

ordered = sorted(
    users,
    key=lambda user: (user["name"].casefold(), user["id"]),
)

print([(user["name"], user["id"]) for user in ordered])
print([1, 2] < [1, 2, 0])
support.caption: Lexicographic tuple keys apply each field in order, so the ID resolves equal normalized names.

beats.recallRule: Compare from left to right: the first unequal pair decides, and an exact shorter prefix comes first.

sections.title: The first difference carries the decision
sections.content:
Lexicographic ordering is the same principle used for words in a simple dictionary: compare positions until one differs. Nested sequences participate recursively, so a tuple of sort fields can express primary, secondary, and later tie-breakers without a custom comparison function.

Element compatibility matters only when Python reaches that pair. `[1, 'x'] < [2, object()]` is decided by `1 < 2` and never compares the later elements. In `[1, 'x'] < [1, 2]`, Python reaches `'x' < 2` and raises `TypeError`.

A sort key can normalize or transform values before comparison while keeping the original records as the returned items.

sections.title: Trace a lexicographic comparison
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Compare elements at position 0] --> B{Equal?}
  B -- No --> C[That pair decides the result]
  B -- Yes --> D[Advance to next position]
  D --> E{One sequence ended?}
  E -- No --> A
  E -- Yes --> F[Shorter sequence sorts first; both ended means equal]
```

sections.title: Sort by family name, then stable ID
sections.content:
```python
users = [
    {"id": 3, "last_name": "Singh"},
    {"id": 2, "last_name": "ada"},
    {"id": 1, "last_name": "Ada"},
]

ordered = sorted(
    users,
    key=lambda user: (user["last_name"].casefold(), user["id"]),
)
print([(user["last_name"], user["id"]) for user in ordered])
# [('Ada', 1), ('ada', 2), ('Singh', 3)]

print([1, 2] < [1, 2, 0])  # True: shorter equal prefix
```

sections.title: Stop at the first difference
sections.content: To compare `(2, 10, 99)` and `(2, 11, 0)`, ignore the final elements: the equal first pair advances to `10 < 11`, which decides the result.
